articles.title: 'Outright corruption': Critic warns Trump's about to spend $1B on 'absurdly niche' fixes
articles.description: President Donald Trump's "dream home" was subjected Thursday to a scathing critique from an infuriated MS NOW analyst who decried the big cash involved in fixing "absurdly niche" problems. "Trump is well on his way to converting the people’s house into his own billion-dollar dream home," MS NOW's Hayes Brown wrote. "It’s a mismanagement of funds at best, outright corruption at worst and ought to prompt legislators to place stricter limits on how and when public funds are rerouted." The price tag for Trump's overhaul of the White House grounds has climbed past $900 million — a figure well beyond what the administration previously disclosed and far above what Congress typically budgets for upkeep of the Executive Mansion. The Washington Post traced $875 million funneled into a normally modest "White House Repair and Restoration" account – $500 million transferred from the Secret Service and the White House Military Office, $305 million from private donors and $70 million from an unidentified source. Brown warned that figure was likely to balloon, "Through shady donations from wealthy funders and corporations, questionable accounting practices and an entirely misplaced sense of focus ." Separately, a contractor's estimate for the ballroom alone reportedly reached $600 million, triple the administration's original $200 million figure and above the $400 million it has said donors covered. The largest and most visible project is a new ballroom being built where the East Wing once stood, though a federal appeals court recently blocked further above-ground construction. Other work underway includes a helipad on the South Lawn, renovated fountains at Lafayette Park, a new visitor screening center and an underground bunker — the last of which the administration has cited in court filings as a national-security rationale for the ballroom project. "One could at least argue that the helipad solves a problem, albeit an absurdly niche one," wrote Brown. "The newest helicopters slated to serve as Marine One have exhaust vents that aim heat downward. The helipad would prevent those vents from scorching the grass below — and boy, does Trump care a lot about grass." The projects are largely cosmetic compared with past White House overhauls, Brown wrote. The Truman-era renovation, prompted by fears the building could collapse, cost roughly $80 million in today's dollars, while the Obama administration spent about $375 million over four years on structural and electrical repairs. "What we see, then, is a White House that feels comfortable pirating funds that Congress has otherwise appropriated to pay for unnecessary vanity projects, Brown wrote. "Without further pushback from lawmakers and the courts, there’s little limit to how much more could be siphoned off to satisfy Trump’s obsession. These rushed and unauthorized works have already vastly outstripped their initial estimates, and given this administration’s love of no-bid contracts , they are being done without a modicum of care for anything but speed."

articles.title: 'A service to the world': Norwegian minister praises Pakistan's leadership for US-Iran mediation efforts
articles.description: Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide reiterated his country’s appreciation of Pakistan’s mediatory role in the ongoing US-Iran conflict on Thursday, saying it was a “service to the world and, hence, also to us”. Eide, who is on a two-day visit to Pakistan, expressed these views while addressing a press conference alongside Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar in Islamabad. “I also really want to reiterate our strong support for the very important role that Pakistan has taken in this dramatic war that started on February 28 with the US-Israel attack on Iran,” he said, recalling that Norway was one of the Western countries that was “clearest and earliest” in stating that the war was a violation of international rules. “If we stand up for international law, it has to apply to everyone, everywhere, all the time,” he stressed. He said that while Norway had “significant disagreements with Iran on other issues, they also have the right to be protected as a state”. Coming to Pakistan’s mediatory role in the ongoing conflict, he said he realised how hard mediation and facilitation of parleys between the two sides could be. “I know what a massive task you were taking on when you offered Islamabad not only as the venue but also as the facilitator of these talks,” he said, lauding Pakistan’s civilian and military leadership for their efforts. “What you have been doing is really a service to the world, and hence, also to us.” He had commended Islamabad’s mediation efforts after his arrival in the federal capital earlier in the day and as he held delegation-level talks with Dar, according to the Foreign Office (FO). The visiting dignitary recognised Pakistan’s role as “important and constructive”, the FO said. “The Norwegian foreign minister commended Pakistan’s important and constructive role during the recent Iran-US conflict, including the leadership and contributions of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, DPM Dar and Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir,” it said. Both sides reviewed the whole gamut of bilateral cooperation in various fields, including trade, investment, climate change, maritime affairs and education. They recognised the important role of the Pakistani diaspora in Norway and agreed to strengthen people-to-people ties between the two countries, it added. The two sides expressed satisfaction at the warm and cordial state of Pakistan-Norway relations and agreed to further deepen cooperation in areas of mutual interest,” it said. The FO said the two sides also held in-depth discussions on regional and international developments of mutual interest. In televised remarks, Eide appreciated Pakistan’s efforts to promote peace and expressed Norway’s desire to further strengthen bilateral ties. He said Norway and Pakistan had a “very strong bilateral partnership”, adding that the presence of a large Pakistani community in Norway, which was “well integrated into Norwegian society”, had helped strengthen ties between the two countries. “There are many leading politicians in Norway and many close colleagues who are actually of Pakistani-Norwegian descent, so it has really made a mark,” he said. Eide said business ties between the two countries were also growing, particularly in the energy and fertiliser sectors, with Norwegian companies increasingly looking at opportunities in Pakistan. He said Norway also saw opportunities for Pakistan to strengthen economic relations through its cooperation with Switzerland and Iceland, noting that the three countries could provide further avenues for expanding business relations. Turning to the regional situation, Eide strongly commended the actions taken by Pakistan’s leadership, including the prime minister and foreign minister, in efforts to promote peace in the Middle East. Eide described the ongoing war as “incredibly dangerous” for global peace as well as the world economy, and praised Pakistan for stepping forward. He also appreciated Pakistan’s role in facilitating the Islamabad talks and maintaining engagement with the parties involved. “I think it is fair to say that the position of Pakistan on the world stage, also in peacemaking, has really been strengthened by this commitment,” he said. Eide said Norway was ready to assist Pakistan’s peace efforts, noting that Oslo had experience in peace negotiations and maintained open dialogue with both Tehran and Washington. “Wherever we can be useful, we will,” he said. He also highlighted Norway’s experience in international maritime affairs, saying the country was among the world’s major seafaring nations despite its relatively small population. He said Norway could therefore play a constructive role in discussions concerning international maritime law and developments surrounding the Strait of Hormuz. Dar, Eide discuss bilateral ties Earlier, the two ministers held a “restricted-format meeting”. “DPM Dar warmly welcomed Eide to Pakistan. The two ministers discussed the full range of bilateral relations, as well as regional and international developments, and reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening bilateral cooperation in all areas of mutual interest,” it said. Upon his arrival in Islamabad, Eide was received at the airport by Additional Foreign Secretary (Europe) Ambassador Ayesha Ali. In a statement on Wednesday, the FO said the minister is undertaking the visit from Aug 13-14 at Dar’s invitation. The visit is the first by a Norwegian foreign minister in a decade, the FO said, adding that the visit would build on high-level engagement between the two countries, including phone conversation between Dar and Eide in March and April , and the visit of Norway’s State Secretary Andreas Motzfeldt Kravik to Islamabad in May. The FO stated that the visit would provide an opportunity to “further strengthen the longstanding and cordial relations between Pakistan and Norway and to explore new areas of mutually beneficial cooperation”.
